source.title: Measuring and Eliminating Refusals in Military Large Language Models
source.authors: Jack FitzGerald; Dylan Bates; Aristotelis Lazaridis; Aman Sharma; Vincent Lu; Brian King; Yousif Azami; Sean Bailey; Jeremy Cao; Peter Damianov; K. de Haan; Joseph Madigan; Jeremy McLaurin; Luke Kerbs; Jonathan Tainer; Dave Anderson; Jonathan Beck; Jamie Cuticello; Colton Malkerson; Tyler Saltsman

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies Heretic abliteration as a weight edit and measures refusal-related behavior and task performance. This tests practical removal, but it does not reproduce the original activation-level projection intervention.
record.gate_note: Rows below cover the study's abliteration results relevant to V2. The paper also reports refusal benchmarks across many other models, judge agreement, and benchmark correlations; those results do not apply or test the ablation and are not included as rows. The difference-in-means formula is described, but its activation-level intervention is not tested here.
record.test_reason: The study applies Heretic abliteration, a weight edit built on the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, to a military-tuned gpt-oss-20b model. It measures refusal and answer rates on three new military refusal benchmarks across many ablation strengths, plus military and general task performance. It also evaluates a third-party abliterated Gemma 3 12B checkpoint. This is V2 tested in a new setting (military domain, private benchmarks), so T3 fits better than T2. The method is not different: the paper's own equations restate the original weight orthogonalization, with Heretic's layerwise weighting.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors call abliteration a stopgap that reduces military refusals: a 66.5-point answer-rate gain costs an average 2% on military tasks. Reaching answer rates in the high 90s needs 10–30% regressions, which they call unacceptable. They also show a general-purpose abliterated Gemma regresses substantially despite low KL. They argue full elimination needs post-training (and perhaps mid-training) without safety data.
record.recipe_differences: The paper defines directional ablation using a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means vector, but applies Heretic weight edits to output-projection matrices rather than projecting activations out at every layer and position. Heretic selects layerwise weights using an iterative optimization procedure and default calibration datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome changes with the Heretic calibration refusal-rate setting: answer rates and military/general task regressions vary across ablation levels. The authors also report that regression differs by task and benchmark.
record.problems: The military evaluation datasets are private, though the paper gives their sizes and says the methods can be requested for audit. Heretic uses default calibration datasets rather than the military tasks. The authors report task-dependent regressions and caution that semantic distance from calibration data may limit interpretation. Table captions indicate p-value-based significance marking, but exact p-values are not supplied in the extracted table text.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports many individual task-score changes for EdgeRunner 20B at each ablation level in Tables 4 and 5; only selected calibration settings and aggregate military/general measures, plus the stated GPQA Diamond result, are included. Other model refusal benchmark scores in Table 2 are baseline evaluations rather than ablation outcomes and are not cataloged here.

untested.parts: Only one model was abliterated by the authors (EdgeRunner 20B), plus one third-party Gemma checkpoint. There is no comparison with the original single-direction weight orthogonalization, and no check of which direction or layers Heretic chose.
No activation-level ablation, no direction-addition experiment, no direction analysis.
Not tested. The authors only argue that post-training without safety data would avoid refusals.

EdgeRunner 20B is a gpt-oss-based reasoning model, and the authors note reasoning lengths were unchanged after abliteration. They do not analyse whether the direction behaves differently in reasoning models.

missing.what: 10% calibration setting: 93.1% gold answer rate with -14.3% military and -5.6% general regression. The text quotes this as the cost of a 93% answer rate.
missing.locator: Section 4 text; Tables 4–5, row with 10% calibration refusal

missing.what: Per-benchmark regressions: truthfulqa falls by up to 21.8%, gsm8k shows no significant regression at any level, and C130 falls 16.2% at the 49% setting while combatmedic-silver is unchanged.

Threshold behaviour: answer rates stay near baseline down to 89% calibration refusal, then jump to 29.6 at 87%. The gold answer rate also falls at the most aggressive settings (84.5 at 6%, 82.7 at 4%), so removal is non-monotonic.

record.verdict_notes: Answer rate is a valid inverse refusal measure here, but the refusal judge uses string markers plus an LLM judge, and the benchmarks are private. Heretic tunes per-layer ablation weights against default (non-military) calibration sets. Table rows are therefore optimizer trials along a refusal/KL trade-off, not independent conditions. The Gemma checkpoint was made by a third party. EdgeRunner 20B is a reasoning model (gpt-oss base), so these results incidentally show weight-edit abliteration working in a reasoning model. The rows were not linked to V8 because the study does not analyse reasoning.

versions.untested_parts: No activation-level projection of the difference-in-means direction from every layer and position; no addition/steering experiment; no test of other abilities after that intervention.

The paper tests Heretic weight edits on EdgeRunner 20B and a Gemma 3 12B abliterated checkpoint, not abliteration across a broad set of released models. It does not establish that refusal is eliminated in general.
No test of whether jailbreaks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine subspace, cone, or multiple directions.
No separation or measurement of harmfulness judgments versus refusal decisions.
No transfer test across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
No comparison of refusal training methods, timing, or training data to test whether they determine the presence of a removable direction.
Some benchmarked models reason, but the study does not test the direction or its ablation in reasoning models.

relation.reason: The authors run abliteration themselves and measure answer and refusal rates and capability across about 25 settings.

tranche.reason: New setting: a military-tuned gpt-oss-20b model, new military refusal benchmarks, and a third-party released Gemma checkpoint, with refusal and capability results on V2. The method (Heretic) is an Optuna-tuned, layer-weighted variant of the original weight orthogonalization, not the same procedure, so T1 does not fit.

source_check.notes: V2's text names only refusal removal, so the capability rows (R14-R19, R23-R24) bear on V2 only under the 'practical' reading. Gemma 3 12B baselines differ between Table 2 (41.9/47.5/76.1) and Table 5 (41.8/48.9/76.9). Only the 57% trial is the Table 2 'EdgeRunner 20B Abl'; the other 'Abl' rows are other Heretic trials. The Gemma checkpoint was abliterated by p-e-w, not the authors. There is no random-direction control. The judge is Selene 1 (Llama 3.3 70B), applied after refusal-marker matching.

statements.correction: EdgeRunner 20B at the 15% calibration setting: -11.9% military avg (R15), -5.1% general avg (R18). At the 4% setting: -34.2% military (R16), -10.3% general (R19). p-e-w/gemma-3-12b-it-heretic-v2 against Gemma 3 12B: -12.3% general avg (R23), -27.8% GPQA Diamond (R24), with 7/100 calibration refusals and calibration KL 0.10. Add R19 to the rows cited.
statements.problem: All numbers for this study are right, and all are relative % changes. The rows cited leave out R19, the row that carries the -10.3 general figure at the 4% setting.

statements.correction: gemma-3-12b-it-heretic-v2: GPQA Diamond -27.8% relative to Gemma 3 12B. Calibration KL 0.10 on Heretic's calibration set. Average general-task regression -12.3%.
statements.problem: Correct. The authors' Table 5 caption says regression can be substantial even with low KL. However, 27.8 is a relative % regression and sits next to point-based figures from other studies.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Moderate EdgeRunner 20B abliteration and the Gemma 3 12B abliterated checkpoint
reader_labels.reason: Answer rates increase substantially on the military refusal benchmarks; at the EdgeRunner 20B setting linked to the authors’ 66.5-point answer-rate increase, average military-task regression is -2.0 (R05-R07, R14), and Gemma answer rates are high (R20-R22).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Abliteration settings aiming for very high answer rates, and the reported abliterated Gemma checkpoint
reader_labels.reason: Removal is incomplete on the gold benchmark (R01); more aggressive settings have larger task regressions (R15-R19), and the Gemma checkpoint has a -12.3 average general-task change including -27.8% on GPQA Diamond (R23-R24).
